Find a diagonalization of A, if one exists, when
A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 \amp -2 \\ 6 \amp -5 \\ \end{array}\right] .

Can the diagonal matrix
A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp -5 \\ \end{array}\right]
be diagonalized? If so, explain how to find the matrices P and D.

Find a diagonalization of A, if one exists, when
A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} -2 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ 1 \amp -3\amp 0 \\ 2 \amp 0 \amp -3 \\ \end{array}\right] .

Find a diagonalization of A, if one exists, when
A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} -2 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ 1 \amp -3\amp 0 \\ 2 \amp 1 \amp -3 \\ \end{array}\right] .

Suppose that A=PDP^{-1} where
D = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp -1 \\ \end{array}\right],\qquad P = \left[\begin{array}{cc} \vvec_2 \amp \vvec_1 \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 \amp 2 \\ 1 \amp -1 \\ \end{array}\right] .
Explain why A is invertible.
Find a diagonalization of A^{-1}.
Find a diagonalization of A^3.

We find that A has eigenvectors \vvec_1=\twovec11 with associated eigenvalue \lambda_1=1 and \vvec_2=\twovec{1}{3} with associated eigenvalue \lambda_2=-3. We then have P=\mattwo1113 and D=\mattwo100{-3}.

Yes. We know that the eigenvectors are \vvec_1=\twovec10 with associated eigenvalue \lambda_1=2 and \vvec_2=\twovec01 with associated eigenvalue \lambda_2=-5. Therefore, P = \left[\begin{array}{rr}\vvec_1 \amp \vvec_2 \end{array}\right] = \mattwo1001=I and D=\mattwo200{-5}=A. This shows that the diagonalization is A=IAI^{-1}; that is, since A is already diagonal, it is diagonalized by the identity matrix.

We find eigenvectors \vvec_1=\threevec112, \vvec_2=\threevec010, and \vvec_3=\threevec001 with associated eigenvalues \lambda_1=-2, \lambda_2=-3, and \lambda_3=-3. Therefore, A = PDP^{-1} where
P = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ 1 \amp 1 \amp 0 \\ 2 \amp 0 \amp 1 \\ \end{array}\right], D = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} -2 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp -3 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp -3 \\ \end{array}\right]\text{.}

Once again, we see that \lambda=-2 is an eigenvalue with multiplicity one and \lambda=-3 is an eigenvalue with multiplicity two. However, \dim E_{-3} = 1 so we are not able to find a basis for \real^3 consisting of eigenvalues of A. Therefore, A is not diagonalizable.

If A=PDP^{-1},
A is invertible since \det A = \det D = -3.
We know that \vvec_1 and \vvec_2 are eigenvectors of A with associated eigenvalues \lambda_1=3 and \lambda_2=-1. If \vvec is an eigenvector of A with associated eigenvalue \lambda, then \vvec is an eigenvector of A^{-1} with associated eigenvalue \frac1{\lambda}. Therefore, A^{-1} = PEP^{-1} where E = \mattwo{\frac13}00{-1}.
We have A^3=PFP^{-1} where F=\mattwo{27}00{-1}.
